why.t: Work from the flow rather than hunting labels one at a time: the right side carries deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae out to the pulmonary artery, the left takes it from the pulmonary veins out to the aorta. Fix the two structures you are certain of and position constrains the rest.

why.q: Thicker myocardium of left ventricle compared to right ventricle
why.t:
Two pairings, each a pair of opposites: atria receive, ventricles pump; systole contracts, diastole relaxes. Getting either half right forces the other, so check them against each other instead of recalling four separate facts.

The three vessel prompts are the trap, and they are worth slowing down for. All three read “…pumped by the heart to the lungs and body tissues through”, so the only thing telling them apart is the first word. The key wants the lung's two blood supplies: deoxygenated → pulmonary artery (blood going to the alveoli to be oxygenated) and oxygenated → bronchial artery (blood going to feed the lung tissue itself, branching off the aorta). The unqualified one is just arteries. If you answered “aorta” in your head for the oxygenated one you were not wrong about the body — the aorta is simply not on the list, because this line is asking about the lung.

why.q: Ligamentum arteriosum
why.t: The heart sounds are valves closing, not opening: LUB is the atrioventricular valves at the start of ventricular systole, DUB the semilunars at the end. The embryonic remnants pair the same way — fossa ovalis is the closed interatrial opening, ligamentum arteriosum the closed duct, and a duct that fails to close is patent.

why.q: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the
why.t: The coronary openings sit just above the aortic valve cusps, so the coronaries fill during diastole, when the valve shuts and blood falls back against it. That is why a very fast heart rate, which shortens diastole, starves the myocardium.

why.q: The two branches of the left coronary artery
why.t: The names describe the route each vessel takes: the left anterior descending runs down the front in the interventricular groove, the circumflex curves around the left side in the atrioventricular groove.

why.q: The branches of the left coronary artery supply the left atrium
why.t: Follow the vessel: the left anterior descending runs down the front of the heart, so left coronary territory includes the anterior ventricular wall. Lung tissue is supplied by bronchial arteries, never by coronaries.

why.q: The branches of the right coronary are the marginal artery and the
why.t: Mirror the left side: the right coronary gives a marginal branch along the right border and a posterior interventricular branch down the back groove. The circumflex belongs to the left, so it cannot appear on this list.

why.q: These branches of the right coronary artery supply the posterior ventricular walls
why.t: The right coronary supplies the right side and the posterior surface, and its marginal branch is named for the right margin it runs along. Left lateral wall is circumflex territory.

why.q: The venous return from the myocardium is through the coronary veins
why.t: Cardiac veins do not join the vena cava. They drain into the coronary sinus in the posterior atrioventricular groove, which empties straight into the right atrium — so the heart returns its own venous blood to itself, upstream of the lungs.

why.q: Which statement is false regarding the conduction system of the heart
why.t: The conduction system is a hierarchy of pacemakers, not a single one. The sinoatrial node is fastest so it normally sets the rhythm, but the atrioventricular node and the ventricular conducting tissue each have their own slower intrinsic rate and take over if it fails — which is exactly what the word 'totally' denies.

why.q: Label the five components of the conduction system
why.t: Label it as a path, not five separate names: the impulse starts in the sinoatrial node high in the right atrium, is deliberately delayed at the atrioventricular node, runs down the atrioventricular bundle, splits into the bundle branches within the septum, and spreads through the Purkinje fibres. The sequence is the answer.

why.q: An ECG records the
why.t: The electrodes are on the skin, so an ECG can only record electrical events. Sounds need a stethoscope, pressures need a catheter and volumes need imaging — matching instrument to signal settles this without recall.

why.q: Explain what the following waves of the ECG represent
why.t: Three of the four electrical events appear on the trace; atrial repolarisation is buried inside the QRS and never gets a wave of its own. Depolarisation precedes contraction, so P comes before atrial systole and QRS before ventricular systole.

why.q: Which ONE of the following can it NOT show
why.t: An ECG records electrical activity, so it detects anything disturbing rhythm or conduction. A leaking or narrowed valve is a mechanical fault — it shows on echocardiography or as a murmur, and only reaches the ECG indirectly, once chambers have enlarged in response.

why.q: A blood pressure of 160/90 in the arteries
why.t: Sort these by what defines each term, not by the numbers. High versus low is a magnitude call; orthostatic is defined by its trigger — standing up — rather than by any particular reading; and primary or essential means no underlying cause was found, which is a statement about aetiology, not about pressure.

why.q: Which formula shows the relationship between BP, CO & SVR
why.t: Pressure is flow times resistance — the circulatory form of Ohm's law. Read it as a lever: raise either output or resistance and pressure rises, which is precisely the two places every antihypertensive drug works.

why.q: The normal heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output for a 70Kg man
why.t: The arithmetic is the check: 70 beats/min × 70 mL is about 4,900 mL, so roughly 5 litres a minute — near enough the whole blood volume every minute at rest. Hold any two of the three and the third is forced.

why.q: The cardiac reserve is the difference between cardiac output
why.t: Two ratios that are easy to swap. Cardiac reserve compares resting output with maximum output — how much more the heart could do. Ejection fraction compares stroke volume with the volume the ventricle held before contracting — how completely it empties on one beat.

why.q: What will happen to SV if the force of contraction
why.t: Contractility is force at a given filling volume, so a stronger squeeze empties the ventricle more completely and stroke volume rises. This is inotropy, and it is separate from preload — nothing about the volume arriving has changed.

why.q: What will happen to SV if arterial vessels are constricted
why.t: Afterload is the pressure the ventricle must overcome before the aortic valve will open. Raise it and the ventricle ejects less per beat for the same effort — which is why untreated hypertension eventually wears the left ventricle out.

why.q: Match the following terms to their definitions
why.t: The trap is per beat against per minute: stroke volume is one beat's worth, cardiac output a minute's worth. Pressure terms describe force against the wall, volume terms describe how much moves — sort each item into force or volume first and the matching falls out.

why.q: The structure of the artery differs from that of a vein
why.t: Arteries take the pulse straight from the ventricle, so they need a thick tunica media and a prominent elastic lamina to stretch and recoil with each beat. Veins carry the same volume at low pressure, so they get thinner walls, wider lumens and valves instead.

why.q: On the arterial side of a capillary bed, filtration is favored
why.t: One pressure changes along the capillary and the other barely does. Hydrostatic pressure falls from the arterial to the venous end while oncotic pressure stays roughly constant — so the balance tips from pushing fluid out to drawing it back in without either force having to reverse.

why.q: Match the causes of edema and the mechanisms
why.t: Every cause acts through one of the four Starling terms: raise capillary hydrostatic pressure, drop plasma oncotic pressure, make the wall leaky, or block lymphatic drainage. Name which term a given cause moves and the matching becomes mechanical.

why.q: The RAAS system is an indirect renal mechanism regulating blood pressure
why.t: The cascade is two enzymes and two hormones in a fixed order: renin makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen, ACE converts that to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II then triggers aldosterone and ADH. Renin and ACE are the enzymes — treating either as a hormone puts the step in the wrong place.

why.q: ACE inhibitors are medications that modify the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone pathway
why.t: The name states the target: they block the enzyme, not the receptor, so angiotensin II is never formed at all. Less angiotensin II means less vasoconstriction and less aldosterone, which is why both pressure and sodium retention fall.

why.q: A coronary angiogram is a medical imaging scanning procedure
why.t: The dye is the whole point: blood and soft tissue absorb X-rays almost identically, so a vessel is invisible until contrast fills its lumen. What the image shows is the shape of the blood column — a narrowing or a blockage — rather than the vessel wall itself.

why.q: The human heart has 3 chambers
why.t: Four chambers, and the reason is the double circuit: two atria receive and two ventricles pump, one side to the lungs and one to the body. Three-chambered hearts belong to animals that tolerate mixing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood.

why.q: This septum is incomplete before birth
why.t: Fetal lungs are collapsed and not yet in use, so blood is shunted past them through the foramen ovale in the interatrial septum. It closes at birth and leaves the fossa ovalis — the shallow depression still visible in an adult heart.

why.q: the aortic valve has ostia
why.t: Both semilunar valves have three pockets and look much alike, so identify them by what lies immediately above the cusps. Only the aorta carries the coronary openings — the heart takes its own supply at the first opportunity.

why.q: also known as the mitral valve because it resembles the mitre of a bishop
why.t: The mitre belongs to the left: two cusps, like a bishop's hat. The right atrioventricular valve has three and is the tricuspid — the name is a cusp count, and the right side has one more.

why.q: Another name for the epicardium is the visceral pericardium
why.t: One membrane with two names, depending on which structure you are describing it as part of — the outer layer of the heart wall, or the inner (visceral) layer of the pericardial sac. The parietal layer is the one lining the fibrous sac itself.

why.q: Which statement is false regarding the Carina
why.t: The carina is a ridge of cartilage at the tracheal bifurcation, and cartilage contains no muscle, so it cannot contract. Everything else on the list follows from it being the most cough-sensitive point in the airway.

why.q: The mucociliary escalator does NOT include
why.t: The escalator needs cilia to sweep and goblet cells to make mucus, so it exists only where the epithelium is ciliated — as far down as the bronchioles. Alveoli are single-cell-thin squamous surfaces built for diffusion; cilia and mucus there would obstruct the very exchange they exist for.

why.q: The bronchial tree consists of
why.t: The tree is the conducting airway — the branching tubes that move air without exchanging any gas. Alveolar sacs are where exchange happens, making them the destination rather than part of the tree.

why.q: You cannot kill yourself by holding your breath
why.t: The drive to breathe is built on rising CO₂, not falling oxygen, and it becomes irresistible long before oxygen runs low. If it were somehow resisted, consciousness is lost first — at which point automatic control simply resumes.

why.q: The aortic and carotid bodies also act as baroreceptors
why.t: One word separates them. The bodies are chemoreceptors, sampling oxygen, CO₂ and pH; the sinus and arch hold the stretch-sensitive baroreceptors reading pressure. Same neighbourhood, different sense.

why.q: The chemoreceptors in aortic and carotid bodies are more sensitive to a change in the oxygen
why.t: CO₂ is the routine controller — small rises change ventilation straight away. The oxygen sensors are a reserve, only taking over once arterial PO₂ has fallen a long way, which is why breathing is regulated minute to minute by carbon dioxide.

why.q: The fast acting peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic and carotid bodies
why.t: Divide them by what they sit in. Peripheral bodies sample arterial blood directly, so they can sense oxygen and can respond fast. Central receptors sit behind the blood–brain barrier in CSF, which is why they answer to CO₂ arriving as H⁺, are the slower of the two, and are effectively blind to oxygen.

why.q: Blood pressure is monitored by high-pressure baroreceptors
why.t: They are stretch receptors, so they measure pressure only indirectly, through how far the vessel wall is distended. Their sites guard the two things that matter most — the output to the whole body at the arch, and the supply to the brain at the carotid sinus.

why.q: The juxtaglomerular apparatus with juxtaglomerular cells
why.t: Sort the apparatus by job. The granular (juxtaglomerular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall are the secretory half and release renin; the macula densa is the sensory half, a patch of distal tubule cells reading the sodium content of the filtrate. One releases, one senses.

why.q: Variations in the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid
why.t: CO₂ crosses the blood–brain barrier easily; H⁺ does not. So a rise in blood CO₂ becomes carbonic acid within the CSF, and the central receptors read the resulting pH shift — they detect carbon dioxide by proxy, through acidity.

why.q: The alveolar cell type 2 makes surfactant
why.t: Two cell types, two jobs: type 1 is the thin sheet the gases cross, type 2 is the cuboidal cell that manufactures surfactant. Surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse at the end of expiration — its absence is why very premature infants struggle to breathe.

why.q: Negative pressure between the visceral and parietal layers of the pleura
why.t: Nothing muscular attaches lung to ribcage; the coupling is entirely the negative pressure in the pleural space. Break that seal and the lung recoils inward while the chest springs outward — the bellows still moves, but the lung no longer moves with it.

why.q: Atelectasis: The deflation and collapse of alveoli
why.t: Atelectasis is collapse of alveoli inside the lung, from a blocked airway, external compression or lost surfactant. Keep it apart from pneumothorax, which is air in the pleural space outside the lung — one is a problem with the tissue, the other with the space around it.

why.q: Pneumothorax: Air in the space outside the lung
why.t: Air entering the pleural space destroys the negative pressure holding the lung expanded, so the lung recoils away from the chest wall. The lung tissue itself is undamaged — what has failed is the seal around it.

why.q: The apneustic centre, that promotes inhalation
why.t: The cerebellum has no respiratory centre at all — it coordinates movement. Both the apneustic and pneumotaxic centres lie in the pons, shaping the rhythm the medulla generates. Any statement placing a breathing centre outside the medulla or pons is wrong on that ground alone.

why.q: Surfactant affects ventilation since it enables the alveoli to expand fully
why.t: Read this as a chain rather than three separate claims. Gradients do not drive the bellows; ventilation refreshes alveolar gas and therefore sets the gradients, and exchange then runs down them. The arrow points one way, and reversing it is the error being tested.

model.q: Where in the body are B- and T- lymphocytes made and stored
model.t: The memory hook is B for bone marrow, T for thymus — both cell lines are made in marrow, and only the T cells travel to mature. Write made, mature and stored as separate statements: the marking points are awarded separately for each.

model.q: What is the structure of a lymph nodes
model.t: Three marks, three parts: capsule, contents, function. Adding that a node has more vessels coming in than going out — so flow slows and the macrophages get time to filter it — shows why the structure suits the job.

model.q: Which cells in the body will find antigens in the body
model.t: The phrase worth writing down is antigen presenting cells. Dendritic cells belong in that group too, though the marking points name macrophages and B lymphocytes.

model.q: Which cells will stimulate a full on immune response
model.t: Keep the sequence in the answer: present, then T cells organise, then B cells make antibody. The marks are for the mechanism, not for naming the cells.

Two halves, and the second is the one that gets forgotten under pressure: answer vaccination in general (the antigen without the disease, memory cells stored) and then the mRNA mechanism specifically. Herd immunity is worth a line.

model.q: What is the difference between vaccination and immunisation
model.t: One mark each way: vaccination is the act, immunisation is the result. Noting that immunisation can also follow the infection itself makes the distinction unmistakable — and it is why a vaccine can fail.
